agent_notes: STEPBible glosses בַּיהוָה as 'in Yahweh'. I kept the literal 'in YHWH' in the glosses and the literal layer: the beth is the cause or sphere of the joy, and Radak allows both 'in place of lamed' and the plain sense. The five English versions split between 'rejoice' (KJV, ASV), 'sing' (YLT) and 'be glad' (BBE); the verb is the ringing, vocal shout of רנן, so I kept a sound word ('ring out').

STEPBible's 'he makes ineffectual' and 'he frustrates' are right for the hiphil of פור and נוא (Metzudat Zion ties הניא to Num 30:6 'her father restrains her'). The perfect tense is probably gnomic; YLT renders it past, the others present. I use a perfect-flavoured literal 'has broken' and a present dramatic voice.

אשרי governs both nouns (Metzudat David: 'blessed the nation... blessed the people'). The 'lo' at the end is 'for him' (the LORD), not for the people. Note the entity link on אלהיו also points to YHWH, correctly.

הִבִּיט (from נבט) and רָאָה are Hebrew perfects, which the five English versions render as present tense. The literal layer keeps the perfect ('has looked… has seen'); the dramatic layer uses the present, since Radak reads the verse as a standing truth against Job 22:14.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses הִשְׁגִּיחַ as 'he looks'; I corrected to 'he gazes intently / peers', following Metzudat Zion ('great scrutiny') and keeping it distinct from הִבִּיט in v.13. Rashi equates the two; the Song 2:9 parallel cited by Radak is the only other biblical use of the root in the Hiphil.

יַחַד has two readings: 'alike/in the same way' (KJV, Webster) or 'all together, at once'. Rashi and Radak, citing Rosh Hashanah 18a, take it as 'all at once' (one scrutiny for all); Meiri and Metzudat David lean on 'the one who formed them all'. I chose 'together' in the literal layer and left both senses in the commentary. Radak and Meiri also record a reading of הַיֹּצֵר as 'treasurer' (Zech 11:13) — I mention it but do not adopt it.

עָשׂוֹר is ambiguous: 'ten-stringed [harp]' (Targum, Rashi's 'ten kinds of melody' is different), or a third instrument 'and the ten' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion read a missing 'and'; Ibn Ezra cites Ps 92:4 עֲלֵי עָשׂוֹר וַעֲלֵי נָבֶל). The literal layer keeps 'harp, ten' with a bracket; the dramatic layer follows the ten-stringed reading, which is the most common one (KJV, ASV, YLT).
The KJV renders the same root זמר as 'sing' here, and has 'psaltery' for נֵבֶל, which is a Greek-derived word and not a Hebrew idea. I did not source the KJV claims beyond the packet text.

agent_notes: חִכְּתָה is a Piel of חכה ('to wait, hold out'), a rarer verb than קוה; gloss 'has waited' vs STEPBible 'it waits'. The perfect has present-state force here, so the dramatic layer uses 'waits'. BBE's 'our salvation' for מָגִנֵּנוּ is an error; the Hebrew is 'shield'.
The word-table lists בוֹ as a prefixed pronoun with lemma 'Os3m'; I glossed it simply 'in him'.

הֵיטִיבוּ נַגֵּן is an adverbial hiphil, 'do well, play'. All five English versions render 'skilfully' or 'expertly'; I kept 'do well' in the literal layer. תְּרוּעָה is the war-and-festival shout or trumpet-blast, not just 'a loud noise' (KJV, ASV, BBE flatten it).

כַּנֵּד: MT 'as a heap' (Rashi, Radak, with Ex 15:8 and Josh 3:13). Some ancient witnesses read כַּנֹּאד 'as in a wineskin'; Rashi explicitly separates נֵד from נֹאד. I follow the Masoretic text and mention the variant in the commentary as my own observation, not sourced. Also, תְּהוֹמוֹת is plural 'deeps'; KJV 'the depth' is singular.

agent_notes: Two different verbs for fear: ירא and גור (here 'dread', Malbim: stronger than yirah). I kept two English words. STEPBible's 'let them be afraid' for גור is acceptable; I glossed 'let them dread'. The YLT indicative ('Afraid of Jehovah are all the earth') reads the imperfects as statements; I follow the jussive reading of KJV, ASV and BBE because the psalm is a call to praise.

The tenses: אָמַר (perfect) then wayyiqtol 'and it was', צִוָּה then 'and it stood'. Ibn Ezra notes the perfect/imperfect interchange. The versions split between past ('it was done', KJV) and present (YLT). I render the narrative past in both layers and keep 'it was', not KJV's 'it was done', because the Hebrew has the verb to be.
